title: Use the Workbench
text: The Workbench shows one condition at a time, in three columns: the source on the left, the stage in the middle, and the list of conditions on the right. It opens with Deuteranopia selected, or with the condition named in the page address.

title: Use the Workbench
heading: The source column
text: What the stage shows: Specimen What you see --- --- Interface A small interface mock-up: a header with a Get started button, and a "Palette health" card Palette The ten reference swatches as a strip Image Your own image: drop it on the stage, or select Choose an image With the Image specimen, the stage says "Drop an image on the stage" and "Whatever you drop stays on your machine — the pipeline runs in this tab and nothing is uploaded." To open a condition's floating panel, see [Browse the Catalogue and panels](browse-the-catalogue-and-panels.md). Type a hex colour into the field (up to seven characters, such as E53E3E ). Next to it, "under condition →" shows the colour it becomes. Under the field, ten swatches (the reference strip) each have a Use button that makes that swatch the base colour. A slider from 0 to 100%, with marks for Normal , the condition's clinical default (for example Clinical default 100% ) and Full . The figure above it says how strongly the condition is expressed, for example "100% · full expression". Selecting a condition resets the slider to that condition's clinical default. As the page puts it: "Severity is a dial on the model, not a milder diagnosis." For the colour-vision conditions, choose how the simulation is calculated: Brettel , Viénot or Machado . The note beside the heading describes the method, for example "projection in LMS" (LMS being the three cone types). See [Limits and accuracy](../others/limits-and-accuracy.md) for how the models differ. - Split shows the reference and the simulation side by side. - Simulated only shows just the simulation.

title: Use the Workbench
heading: The stage
text: The heading names what you are looking at, for example "COLOUR TRANSFORM · Deuteranopia · 100%". Under the stage are two readouts. Pairs of reference colours that were comfortably apart (CIEDE2000 of 12 or more) and land within 8 under this condition, ranked by how far they fell. The heading says how many, for example "2 of 45 reference pairs fall under ΔE2000 8", and each pair shows its distance before and after, such as "24 → 1.5". The ten reference swatches make 45 pairs. A pair that collapses is two colours that a person with this condition can no longer tell apart. Measure Meaning --- --- ΔE76 How far the base colour moved, as a simple distance in Lab colour space ΔE2000 How far it moved, with the CIEDE2000 formula, which follows perceived difference more closely pairs lost / 45 How many reference pairs collapsed button label / fill The contrast ratio of the mock-up's button label against its fill, under the condition ΔE (delta E) is a measure of colour difference: around 1 is barely noticeable, and larger numbers mean more obvious differences.

title: Use the Workbench
heading: The conditions column
text: - Search 78 conditions filters the list by name. - Filter buttons: All 78 , Colour (the 17 per-colour transforms), Field (the 61 field effects) and Basic only . - The selected condition is described at the top: its severity score in a ring, its name and category, a one-line description (for example "Green-cone absent. A per-colour transform: every pixel has an answer."), and chips for its kind, its prevalence and its level. - Below, every condition is listed by category, with its severity score. Field conditions are marked FIELD . Select a condition to put it on the stage.

title: Troubleshooting the Vision Lab
text: - Why: the Level filter is set to Basic , which shows only the per-colour conditions. It follows the site-wide Simple/Advanced preference. - What to do: select Filter , then Level › All . - Why: the search and filters together exclude every condition. - What to do: select Clear the filters , or clear the search. - Why: on the free plan you can open 25 simulations a day from the Catalogue, and today's are used. - What to do: use the Workbench , which is not counted, or come back tomorrow. Paid plans have no daily cap. - Why: up to five panels can be open; a sixth replaces the oldest panel that is not pinned. - What to do: select Pin panel on panels you want to keep, or close panels you no longer need. - Why: five panels are open and all five are pinned, or today's free simulations are used. - What to do: unpin or close a panel, or check the daily tally. - Why: Auto-apply to new panels may be off or paused, or the image was loaded before the panels opened. - What to do: open Source image and select Apply to all panels . - Why: Quality is set to Balanced or Full, which processes more pixels. - What to do: choose Fast · 1024px while exploring. - Why: the model applies to the colour-vision conditions. Field conditions, such as glaucoma, are not colour transforms. - What to do: choose a per-colour condition to compare models. - Why: simulations model a typical case on an uncalibrated screen. Real vision varies from person to person, and your display, its settings and the room light all change how colours appear. - What to do: treat the result as a guide, not a measurement. See [Limits and accuracy](../others/limits-and-accuracy.md). - Why: a ?vw= link always opens the Workbench; a v= link restores the Catalogue workspace. - What to do: use Copy link to this view in the Workbench, Copy link in the Catalogue, or Copy link to this sheet in Compare, depending on what you want to share. - Why: your images never leave your device, so they cannot travel in a link. Built-in samples and test charts do. - What to do: send the image separately, or share a built-in sample. - Why: the lab remembers your work in this browser only. A different browser, a private window, or clearing site data starts afresh. - What to do: share important views as links, and export what you need.

title: Vision Lab FAQ
heading: Is it free?
text: Yes. Every simulation is free on every plan. The free plan counts up to 25 simulations a day opened from the Catalogue; paid plans lift that cap. The Workbench, Compare, Palette audit and Analytics are free to use.

title: Vision Lab FAQ
heading: Is it a medical tool?
text: No. The page says: "Educational visualisation only. Not a medical simulation, a diagnostic tool, or a substitute for professional eye care — and screen colours are not calibrated." It cannot diagnose or test anyone's vision.

title: Vision Lab FAQ
heading: Which models does it use?
text: For the colour-vision conditions, the published models of Brettel (1997), Viénot (1999) and Machado (2009), calculated in linear light. You can switch between them in the Workbench and in each panel.

title: Vision Lab FAQ
heading: What is the difference between per-colour and field conditions?
text: A per-colour condition changes each colour in a predictable way, so every colour has an exact answer. A field condition changes how and where you see, such as blur, dark patches or a lost half of the visual field; colour may survive while the field does not.

title: Vision Lab FAQ
heading: What does the severity score mean?
text: It is an estimated visual-impact score from 1 to 10. It orders the collection; it is not a clinical grade and does not rank anyone's sight.

title: Vision Lab FAQ
heading: What does the severity slider do?
text: It sets how strongly the model is applied, from 0 (normal vision) to 100% (full expression). As the page puts it, severity is a dial on the model, not a milder diagnosis.

title: Vision Lab FAQ
heading: How do I check a whole palette?
text: Use Palette audit . It checks every pair of up to 24 colours under all 17 colour conditions and suggests lightness fixes for pairs that merge. See [Audit a palette](audit-a-palette.md).

title: Vision Lab FAQ
heading: Are my images uploaded?
text: No. The page says: "Whatever you drop stays on your machine — the pipeline runs in this tab and nothing is uploaded."

title: Vision Lab FAQ
heading: Can I share what I am looking at?
text: Yes: Copy link to this view (Workbench), Copy link (Catalogue) or Copy link to this sheet (Compare). See [Links, saving and exports](links-saving-and-exports.md).

title: Vision Lab FAQ
heading: How is this different from the Analyzer's Simulation section?
text: The [Analyzer](../../analyzer/README.md) previews a whole web page under six filters. The Vision Lab goes much deeper: 78 conditions, severities, models, measurements, a palette audit and image input.

title: Vision Lab FAQ
heading: Can I automate it?
text: The palette audit is available from the REST API as POST /v1/vision/audit , at 5 API credits per call. See the public API documentation at https://auricartisan.com/library/documentation/api/.

title: Vision Lab glossary
text: Achromatopsia — Seeing no colour at all, only light and dark. CAM (colour appearance model) — A model of how a colour looks in context: under a given light, surround and brightness. The panels offer CAT16, CAM16-UCS, CIECAM02 and Hunt-Stevens options. CIE xy — A two-number description of a colour's hue and saturation (chromaticity), plotted on the CIE 1931 diagram. CIEDE2000 (ΔE2000) — A formula for colour difference that follows human perception closely. Around 1 is barely noticeable. Clinical default — The severity at which a condition is shown by default. Collapse — Two colours that were clearly different becoming indistinguishable under a condition. The Workbench counts a reference pair as collapsed when it was 12 or more apart and falls within 8 (CIEDE2000). Cone — A light-sensitive cell in the eye. L, M and S cones respond to long (red), medium (green) and short (blue) wavelengths. Correlated colour temperature (CCT) — The colour of a white light, in kelvin: lower is warmer, higher is cooler. CVD (colour-vision deficiency) — Reduced ability to tell some colours apart, often called colour blindness. Deuteranopia, protanopia, tritanopia — Colour-vision deficiencies in which the green-, red- or blue-sensitive cones are absent. Deuteranomaly, protanomaly, tritanomaly — Milder forms, in which those cones are present but weakened. ΔE (delta E) — A measure of colour difference. ΔE76 is a simple distance in Lab colour space; ΔE2000 is the more perceptual CIEDE2000. Field effect — A condition that changes how or where you see (blur, lost regions, glare, distortion) rather than changing each colour. Illuminant — A standard light source used in colour calculations, such as D65 (average daylight). Linear light — Colour values converted from screen encoding to values proportional to light, which the models need to work correctly. LMS — The three cone responses (long, medium, short). Colour-vision models work by adjusting colours in LMS space. Observer (2° or 10°) — The standard field of view assumed by colour maths: 2° for small or close things, 10° for large areas. Per-colour transform — A condition in which each colour becomes another colour in a predictable way. Prevalence — Roughly how common a condition is. Severity — On the slider, how strongly the model is applied (0–100%). As a score, an estimated visual-impact rating from 1 to 10. Specimen — What the Workbench stage shows: the Interface mock-up, the Palette strip or your Image. White point — The colour treated as white under a given light.

title: Limits and accuracy
heading: What the simulations are
text: - Educational visualisations. The page states they are "not a medical simulation, a diagnostic tool, or a substitute for professional eye care". They show how a typical case of a condition might affect what you see, to help design and teaching. - Per-colour conditions use published colour-vision models, calculated in linear light (colours are converted from screen values to values proportional to light before any maths): - Brettel (1997) projects colours onto the plane a dichromat can see, in LMS cone space. - Viénot (1999) is a simplified, single-plane version of the same idea. - Machado (2009) models reduced cone sensitivity, which suits the milder "-anomaly" forms and partial severities. The floating panels label their version "Machado-like". The models agree on the broad picture and differ in detail. Try more than one. - Field conditions are illustrative effects (blur, dimming, lost regions, glare, distortion) drawn over the image. They show the kind of loss, not a measured map of any real patient's field. - Severity is a dial on the model, not a milder diagnosis. The severity score (1 to 10) is an estimated visual-impact score that orders the collection; it is not a clinical grade.

title: Limits and accuracy
heading: What changes the result you see
text: - Your screen. Screen colours are not calibrated. Brightness, colour profile, night modes and panel type all change what you see. - The room. Ambient light changes how colours look. - Your own vision. If you have a colour-vision deficiency yourself, a simulation of another deficiency is filtered through your own. - Real people vary. Two people with the same diagnosis can see differently.

title: Limits and accuracy
heading: Measurements
text: - ΔE76 and ΔE2000 are calculated between the original and simulated colours. ΔE2000 follows perception more closely. - Collapse in the Workbench and Compare means a reference pair that was at least 12 apart (ΔE2000) falls within 8. Palette audit uses your chosen threshold, 5 by default. - Button label / fill and CTA figures are WCAG contrast ratios, calculated on the simulated colours of the mock-up. - Palette audit covers the 17 per-colour conditions only; field conditions are not colour transforms.

title: Limits and accuracy
heading: Images
text: - Images are processed at a working size set by Quality (1024, 1600 or 4096 pixels), not always at full resolution. - Very large images take longer at the higher quality settings.

title: Limits and accuracy
heading: What the lab is not
text: - Not a vision test or a diagnosis. - Not a guarantee that a design is accessible. Pair it with contrast checks and with testing by people who have these conditions. - Not a substitute for professional eye care.

title: Vision Lab privacy
heading: Your images stay on your device
text: The page says it plainly: "Whatever you drop stays on your machine — the pipeline runs in this tab and nothing is uploaded." Every simulation, measurement and audit runs in your browser.

title: Vision Lab privacy
heading: What is kept in your browser
text: - the view you last used, and the Workbench's condition, severity, model, specimen and base colour; - the Catalogue category, your favourites, the Compare sheet and the Palette audit palette; - the panels you had open, their snapshots, and the position of the Vision Control dock. Clearing this site's data in your browser removes all of it.

title: Vision Lab privacy
heading: The daily count
text: On the free plan, the lab counts how many simulations you open from the Catalogue each day, and the count is also checked by Auric Artisan. Only the count is involved; your colours and images are not sent.

title: Vision Lab privacy
heading: Links
text: A workspace link ( v= ) and a Workbench link ( ?vw= ) carry your settings in the address, readable by anyone who has the link. They never contain your own images. The site-wide privacy policy is covered in [Company and legal](../../../../company-and-legal/README.md).

title: ASCII Art Generator
text: The ASCII Art Generator turns a picture into character art: rows of letters, symbols, blocks or Braille dots whose density follows the light and dark of the image. You drop in a photo, a screenshot or a logo, or type a word, and the art appears straight away and updates as you change anything. Five ready-made looks cover most needs. Behind Fine tuning sit the controls that decide how the picture is read: seven character sets or your own ramp, the cell shape, brightness model, gamma and contrast, three sampling methods, Floyd–Steinberg and Bayer dithering, edge-aware glyph choice, the output font, filters such as flip, rotate and frame, and a seed. The art can be shown as plain text, colour HTML, a canvas image or SVG. Everything happens in your browser. Pictures are read and converted on your device and are not uploaded. You can copy the art, or download it as TXT, PNG, SVG, HTML, JSON, CSV or a colour ANSI file for terminals. An Analysis tab and a Compare tab measure the character sets and the render for anyone who wants to know why the art looks the way it does.

title: ASCII Art Generator
heading: Who it is for
text: - Developers who want a banner for a README, a terminal or a commit message. - Designers and artists making text-based artwork or retro graphics. - Teachers and students exploring how images are sampled and dithered. - Anyone who wants a picture of themselves, a pet or a logo in characters.

title: Getting started with the ASCII Art Generator
heading: The layout
text: Four tabs: Lab , Analysis , Compare and Export . You do almost everything in Lab . Lab has two parts: - The control rail on the left: - Source : Image , Text or Webcam , and the controls for the one you pick; - Look : five named looks, a strip showing the characters in use from Light to Dark , and their count, such as 10 glyphs ; - Colour : Mono or From image , and in Mono the Ink and Paper colours; - Detail : how many characters wide the art is, and Invert for dark paper ; - Fine tuning : a button that opens every other setting, in folded groups. - The stage on the right: Render chips ( Text , HTML , Canvas , SVG ) and the render time, the art itself, and a footer with Grid , Chars , Render , Copy and Full screen . Select any group heading in the rail to fold it away or open it again. On screens narrower than about 1,180 pixels the stage comes first and the controls follow below it.

title: Getting started with the ASCII Art Generator
heading: The empty stage
text: Before you give it anything, the stage reads Drop an image on the stage and offers four buttons: Choose a file , Try an example , Type some text and Use the webcam . Under them, Your ramp, right now previews how the current character set draws a gradient.

title: Getting started with the ASCII Art Generator
heading: Your first piece
text: 1. Select Try an example . The tool draws a lit sphere and converts it. 2. Under Look , select Blocks , then Line art , and watch the art change. 3. Drag Detail to about 160. 4. Under Colour , select From image . The render switches to HTML and each character takes its colour from the picture. 5. Select Full screen to see it large, then close it with × . 6. Under Colour , select Mono again, and select Copy . The message Copied! confirms the text is on your clipboard. Result: a piece of plain-text art ready to paste into a document, a chat or a code comment. There is no Render button. The art converts as soon as you give it a source and again shortly after each change.

title: Charts, benchmark and Compare
text: The Analysis and Compare tabs explain why the art looks the way it does. You do not need them to make art; they help when a result bands, looks flat or converts slowly.

title: Charts, benchmark and Compare
heading: The Analysis tab
text: The left column repeats the facts of the last conversion: - Grid , Characters and Render (time in milliseconds); - Character set , and Ramp (the number of glyphs, for example 10 glyphs ); - Sampler and Dithering . Run benchmark converts the current source ten times with the current settings and reports the average, for example Avg: 18.4 ms (10 runs) , and the Min , Max and Spread . Use it to see which setting makes conversion slow. With the Image source and no picture loaded, it reads Load an image first . Six charts. Each has a ⛶ button, and you can also double-click a chart, to open it full screen. Close the full-screen chart with × , Esc , or by selecting the dark background. Chart What it shows What to look for --- --- --- Glyph density calibration The ink of each character in the current set, measured by drawing it at 32 × 32 pixels, sorted light to dark. A smooth rise. Big jumps or flat runs mean some tones have no matching character. Character frequency How often each character appears in the latest output. A spike at one end means gamma or contrast is crushing the mid-tones. Top character distribution The twelve most frequent characters as a ring, with the rest grouped as one slice. Whether a few characters dominate the art. Sobel edge field The strength of edges in the source picture; bright means a strong edge. Where edge-aware glyph selection can act. Where it is dark, Edge weight has nothing to work on. Sampling comparison The same source through area averaging, bilinear and point sampling. Point sampling breaking fine detail into noise. Render timeline Conversion time for the last hundred conversions. Where live updates stop keeping up with the sliders. The charts redraw after every conversion and when you open the tab.

title: Charts, benchmark and Compare
heading: The Compare tab
text: Measure all sets draws every character of all seven sets at 32 × 32 pixels, measures how much ink each one has, and fills a table: Column Meaning --- --- Charset The set: standard, detailed, blocks, minimal, symbols, lines or braille. Glyphs The number of characters, including the space. Min density The ink of the lightest character, from 0 to 1. Max density The ink of the darkest character. Range Max minus min. A wider range carries more contrast. Monotonic ✓ if every character has at least as much ink as the one before it, in the set's own order; ✗ if not. A set that is not monotonic has at least one character darker than the one after it, and a smooth gradient drawn with it shows bands. More glyphs carry more detail; a wider range carries more contrast. They are not the same thing. The measurement uses the fonts on your device, so results can differ slightly between computers. Your custom ramp is not in the table; when it is in use, its densities show in the Glyph density calibration chart.

text: Open the Export tab. Each card has a download button. Card Button File What it contains --- --- --- --- TXT Download .txt ascii-art.txt The characters, one line per row, with filters applied. PNG Download .png ascii-art.png A picture of the art. SVG Download .svg ascii-art.svg Vector art with selectable characters. HTML Download .html ascii-art.html A standalone web page. The only download that keeps colour as coloured text. JSON Download .json ascii-research.json The characters and every setting that produced them. CSV Download .csv ascii-analysis.csv How often each character appears. ANSI Download .ans ascii-art.ans The characters with 24-bit colour codes for terminals. A message confirms each download, for example TXT exported . If nothing has been converted yet, it reads Nothing to export . The PNG, SVG and HTML downloads are built from a render, so choose the matching Render chip on the Lab tab first: For Show this render first Otherwise --- --- --- PNG Canvas The PNG is drawn from the last HTML render if there has been one, or from the text using the output font, Ink and Paper . SVG SVG The SVG reuses the last SVG render or SVG download if there has been one, or wraps the last HTML render, or draws the text in black on white. HTML HTML The page contains the last HTML render if there has been one, or the plain text in black on white. Without that step, a PNG, SVG or HTML download can show an earlier version of the art. See [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md). With an HTML render, the file is a page on a black background holding the coloured characters on your paper colour. It opens in any browser. It records the time, the source (image, text or webcam), the render mode, the characters in the ramp, every option, the text of the art, the timings of the last twenty conversions and the glyph densities. It does not include the source picture. The generator cannot load a JSON file back in; keep it as a record of the settings, or use it in your own code. Three columns, Character , Count and Frequency (per cent), sorted from the most common character down. Line breaks are not counted. The card on the page also mentions density per glyph, but the file holds frequencies only; the densities are in the JSON file. A text file whose colour runs are 24-bit terminal colour codes, with a reset at the end of every line. Print it in a terminal that supports true colour (for example with cat ascii-art.ans on macOS or Linux) and the picture appears in colour. It needs From image colour. With Mono , Download .ans shows Turn colour on first — ANSI carries the image's colours and saves nothing. After a successful download the message reads Saved ascii-art.ans — cat it in a terminal .

title: Copy, export and batch
heading: Export several files at once
text: Export all six , in the left column of Export , downloads five files one after another: the TXT, PNG, SVG, JSON and CSV files. It does not include the HTML or ANSI files; download those from their cards. Your browser may ask whether to allow several downloads from the page.

title: Copy, export and batch
heading: Batch: render a list of words
text: The Batch box takes one line of text per row, for example: AURIC ARTISAN ASCII Render each line converts each line as Text source, with the current text font and conversion settings, and fills Batch results with a table of Input (the first 30 characters), Cols , Rows , Chars and Time (ms) . With nothing in the box it reads No inputs . Batch measures; it does not produce files or change the art on the stage. It does leave the last line of the list in the Text box on the Lab tab.

title: Copy, export and batch
heading: Save to your Library
text: On this page, the Library's Save to Library stores the current art and your settings in your Auric Artisan Library, and opening the item later puts them back. See the [Library Kit](../../../../kits/library-kit/README.md).

title: Fine tuning
text: Select Fine tuning at the bottom of the rail to open eight more groups. Each starts folded; select a group's heading to open it. Every change re-converts the art a moment later. Changing anything here clears the highlight on the Look buttons, since the art no longer matches a named look.

title: Fine tuning
heading: Character set
text: A menu of seven sets, each listed light to dark: Set Characters Count --- --- --- Standard space .:-=+ %@ 10 Detailed space and 69 punctuation marks, letters and digits 70 Blocks space ░▒▓█ 5 Minimal space .: @ 5 Symbols space ·•●◉⬤ 6 Lines space and box-drawing characters ─│┌┐└┘ and more 23 Braille space and all 255 Braille patterns 256 Custom ramp lets you type your own characters, lightest first and darkest last, up to 200. It needs at least two characters; with fewer, the set chosen in the menu is used. Start with a space so the lightest areas stay empty, for example .oO@ . The Look strip in the rail always shows the set actually in use, custom ramp included.

title: Fine tuning
heading: Shape
text: Character cells are taller than they are wide, so without correction the art comes out stretched. Control Range Default What it does --- --- --- --- Match the output font on or off on Measures the output font and sets Cell aspect to match it. Cell aspect 0.2 to 1.2 set by the font Width of a cell divided by its height. Lower values give fewer rows. Lock row count on or off off Fixes the number of rows instead of working it out from the picture. Rows 10 to 300 50 The fixed row count, when locked. Moving Cell aspect by hand works best with Match the output font off; while it is on, choosing another output font measures it again.

title: Fine tuning
heading: Tone
text: Control Range Default What it does --- --- --- --- Brightness model Luminosity (Rec.601) , Average , Lightness (HSL) Luminosity How a pixel's colour becomes a single brightness. Luminosity weights green most, as the eye does. Gamma 0.2 to 3.0 1.0 Above 1 lifts the mid-tones (lighter); below 1 deepens them. Contrast 0 to 1 0 Stretches the picture's contrast before conversion. Saturation 0 to 2 0 Boosts colour before conversion. Mainly affects From image colour.

title: Fine tuning
heading: Sampling
text: Control Options Default What it does --- --- --- --- Sampling method Area average (SAT) , Bilinear , Point / Nearest Area average How the pixels under each cell become one value. Area averaging uses every pixel and is the most faithful; point sampling is fastest but can shimmer on fine detail. Dithering None , Floyd-Steinberg , Ordered (Bayer) None Spreads the rounding error between neighbouring cells so smooth gradients show as texture instead of bands. Bayer matrix Bayer 4×4 , Bayer 8×8 8×8 The pattern size for ordered dithering. Floyd–Steinberg gives an organic, grainy texture; ordered dithering gives a regular cross-hatch.

title: Fine tuning
heading: Edges
text: Control Range Default What it does --- --- --- --- Sobel glyph selection on or off on Finds edges in the picture and, at strong edges, swaps in a thin line character of similar brightness. Edge weight 0 to 1 0.65 How strongly edges steer the choice of character. The line characters it can use are the backtick, - , / , and the backslash, and only those present in the current set. So it has most effect with Detailed , a little with Standard (which has - ), and none with Blocks, Minimal, Symbols, Lines or Braille. The character is chosen by brightness, not by the direction of the edge. The Sobel edge field chart in Analysis shows where the edges are.

title: Fine tuning
heading: Type
text: Control Range Default What it does --- --- --- --- Output font monospace, Courier New, Consolas, Monaco monospace Font of the HTML, Canvas and SVG renders and of downloads. Size 6 to 32 pixels 12 Character size for the Canvas and SVG renders and downloads. Line height 0.8 to 2.0 1.0 Row spacing. Kerning −2 to 4 0 Extra space between characters, in pixels. Render mode Text (plain) , HTML (color spans) , Canvas (rasterised) , SVG (vector) Text The same choice as the Render chips above the art. On screen, the Text and HTML renders are scaled to fit the stage whatever size you choose.

title: Fine tuning
heading: Filters
text: Eight check boxes, applied to the finished characters: Filter Effect --- --- Flip X Mirrors left to right. Flip Y Mirrors top to bottom. Rotate 90° Turns the art a quarter turn clockwise. Border Surrounds the art with . Frame Surrounds the art with a double-line box. Brighten Moves each Standard-set character one step towards @ . Darken Moves each Standard-set character one step towards a space. Noise Replaces a share of the characters with random Standard-set characters. Noise amount (0 to 1, default 0.1) sets that share. Filters work on the characters, not the picture, so: - Brighten , Darken and Noise use the Standard characters; with other sets, Brighten and Darken leave characters they do not know unchanged, and Noise mixes Standard characters in; - the HTML render does not show filters at all, although Copy and the TXT download include them; - with From image colour, shape-changing filters ( Rotate 90° , Border , Frame ) make the Canvas and SVG renders fall back to one colour, and the flips can leave colours in their original places.

title: Fine tuning
heading: Advanced
text: Control Range Default What it does --- --- --- --- Thin out 0 to 0.95 0 Drops characters from runs of the same character. Lines become shorter, so the picture skews; use it for effect, not to save space. Seed a whole number 2654435769 Fixes the random choices of Noise and the position of the ordered-dither pattern, so the same seed gives the same result.

heading: Related
text: - [Looks, colour and detail](looks-colour-and-detail.md) - [Charts, benchmark and Compare](charts-and-compare.md) - [Reference](reference.md)

title: Looks, colour and detail
text: The three groups under Source are the ones most people need: Look , Colour and Detail .

title: Looks, colour and detail
heading: Look
text: Five buttons. Each sets a character set and a few tone and edge settings at once, then re-converts the art. Look Character set What it sets --- --- --- Classic Standard Gamma 1, contrast 0.15, edge-aware on, edge weight 0.65 Blocks Blocks Gamma 1, contrast 0.2, edge-aware off Fine Detailed Gamma 1, contrast 0.1, edge-aware on, edge weight 0.5 Bold Minimal Gamma 0.9, contrast 0.45, edge-aware off Line art Standard Gamma 1.4, contrast 0.6, edge-aware on, edge weight 1 Classic is highlighted when the page opens, but its contrast is not applied until you select it. If you change anything in Fine tuning , the highlight clears, because the art no longer matches a named look. Under the buttons, a strip shows the characters in use from Light to Dark , and the heading counts them, for example 10 glyphs . Sets longer than 24 characters are shown as an even sample of 24. - Classic suits most photos. - Blocks gives solid, graphic shading and works well at small sizes. - Fine uses a long ramp of 70 characters and keeps the most tonal detail at large widths. - Bold uses only four marks and a space, for strong, poster-like art. - Line art pushes contrast and edges, for logos, drawings and outlines.

title: Looks, colour and detail
heading: Colour
text: Two buttons: - Mono : every character in one colour. The Ink and Paper colour wells appear. The render switches to Text . - From image : each character takes the colour of the part of the picture it stands for. Ink and Paper are hidden, and the render switches to HTML , which can show colour. After choosing From image you can also switch to the Canvas or SVG render; both keep the colour. See [Render modes and full screen](render-modes.md). Ink defaults to f0f0f0 (near white) and Paper to 0f0e0c (near black). - Paper is the background of the HTML , Canvas and SVG renders, and of their downloads. - Ink is the character colour of the Canvas and SVG renders in Mono. - A PNG download made while the Text render is showing uses both. - The Text render on screen ignores them and uses the page's own colours, and a Mono HTML render uses the page's text colour on your paper. With From image , the paper colour is still used as the background.

title: Looks, colour and detail
heading: Detail
text: The Detail slider sets the width of the art in characters, from 20 to 300 (default 100); the heading shows it, for example 100 wide . The number of rows follows from the picture's proportions and the cell shape, unless you lock the row count in Fine tuning (see [Fine tuning](fine-tuning.md)). - 60 to 120 columns suit a README, a chat message or a terminal window. - 150 to 300 columns keep more detail but need a small font or a wide screen to look right. On screen the art is scaled to fit the stage, so a wider setting shows smaller characters, not a larger picture. The character sets run from the least ink (a space) to the most. On light paper, a dark part of the picture should get the most ink; on dark paper it should get the least. Invert for dark paper flips the mapping. The tool sets it for you: it turns on while Paper is dark and off while it is light. Once you select the box yourself, it stays as you set it.

title: Looks, colour and detail
heading: Related

title: Render modes and full screen
text: The Render chips above the art choose how it is shown. The characters are the same in every mode; what changes is how they are drawn and what they can carry.

title: Render modes and full screen
heading: The four renders
text: Chip Shows the art as Colour Filters Best for --- --- --- --- --- Text Plain characters in the page's text colour No Yes Copying and pasting HTML Characters in coloured runs on your paper colour Yes No Colour art on screen and the HTML download Canvas A picture drawn at the output font and size Yes Yes A pixel-exact PNG SVG Vector text, one line per row Yes Yes Scalable art and the SVG download - Colour means the render can show From image colour. See [Looks, colour and detail](looks-colour-and-detail.md). - Filters means the render shows the filters from Fine tuning . The HTML render always shows the art before filters. - Choosing From image switches to HTML , and choosing Mono switches back to Text . You can pick another chip afterwards. The Text and HTML renders are scaled to fit the stage. The Canvas and SVG renders are drawn at the Size set under Type in Fine tuning , and shrink to fit the stage width if they are wider.

title: Render modes and full screen
heading: The readouts
text: The footer under the art shows: - Grid : columns × rows, for example 100 × 42 ; - Chars : the number of characters; - Render : how long the last conversion took, in milliseconds. The render time also appears beside the Render chips. The Analysis tab repeats these figures with the character set, glyph count, sampler and dithering. See [Charts, benchmark and Compare](charts-and-compare.md).

title: Render modes and full screen
heading: Copy
text: Copy in the footer copies the plain characters to your clipboard, with filters applied, whichever render is showing. The message Copied! confirms it. To copy with colour for a terminal, use Copy for terminal in Export . See [Copy, export and batch](export.md).

title: Render modes and full screen
heading: Full screen
text: Full screen opens the art over the whole window on a dark background. - For the Canvas render, it shows the canvas picture. - For the other renders, it shows the plain characters in gold, without colour. Close it with × in the top-right corner.

title: Choose a source
text: The Source group at the top of the rail has three buttons: Image , Text and Webcam . Switching source converts the new source at once if it has something to show, or returns to the empty stage if it has not.

title: Choose a source
heading: Image
text: Use a photo, screenshot, logo or drawing. Ways to load one: - select the drop area ( Drop an image, or click to browse ) or Choose a file on the empty stage, and pick a file; - drag a file anywhere onto the tool; the stage highlights while you drag; - copy an image and press Ctrl + V ( Cmd + V on a Mac) anywhere on the page, as long as you are not typing in a field; - select Try an example to load a built-in picture of a lit sphere on a dark gradient. Accepted types are PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP, SVG and TIFF, up to 20 MB. Whether TIFF opens depends on your browser. After loading, the rail shows the picture's size, such as 1200 × 800 px . Pictures larger than 4,000 pixels on a side, or larger than 12 megapixels, are scaled down first, and a note says so, for example Downscaled from 6000×4000 to 4000×2667 . The art never needs that much detail, so you will not normally see a difference. Clear removes the picture and returns the stage to its empty state. An animated GIF is converted as a single still frame.

title: Choose a source
heading: Text
text: Select Text (or Type some text on the empty stage) to turn a word or short line into art. Control What it does Default --- --- --- Text box The text to draw. ASCII Font monospace, Courier New, Consolas, Monaco, Fira Code or Source Code Pro. monospace Size 8 to 128 pixels. 48 Weight Normal , Bold or Black . Bold White on black Draws light letters on a dark ground instead of dark on light. off The text is first drawn as a picture in the chosen font, then converted like an image. The font must be installed on your device; if it is not, your browser substitutes another. Bigger sizes give smoother letter shapes; set Detail wide enough to hold them. If the box is empty, the stage returns to its empty state.

title: Choose a source
heading: Webcam
text: Select Webcam (or Use the webcam on the empty stage) to see the camera controls. At the time of writing, the camera cannot be used on auricartisan.com. The site tells browsers not to give any of its pages camera access, so Start does not turn the camera on, and a message under the buttons says that camera permission was denied. Changing the camera permission in your browser does not help. To convert a picture of yourself, take a photo with your camera app and load it with Image . For reference, the controls are: Control What it is for --- --- Start Ask for the camera and show a small live preview. Capture Convert the current frame. Keep converting every frame Convert continuously, several times a second. Smooth between frames Blend each frame a little with the one before, to reduce flicker. Stop Turn the camera off.

title: Troubleshooting
heading: Nothing happens when I open the page
text: That is expected: the stage waits for a source. Choose a file, drop or paste a picture, select Try an example , or switch to Text . There is no Render button; conversion starts by itself.

title: Troubleshooting
heading: My file will not load
text: - Unsupported file type : use PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP, SVG or TIFF. Convert other formats, such as HEIC, first. - File too large : the limit is 20 MB. Save a smaller copy or a JPEG. - Failed to load image : the file may be damaged, or your browser cannot read that format. TIFF in particular opens only in some browsers.

title: Troubleshooting
heading: Pasting a picture does nothing
text: Click on an empty part of the page first, so you are not typing in a field, then press Ctrl + V ( Cmd + V on a Mac). The clipboard must hold an image, not a link to one.

title: Troubleshooting
heading: The webcam will not start
text: At the time of writing, auricartisan.com tells browsers not to allow camera access on any of its pages. Start then shows a message that camera permission was denied. Changing permissions in your browser does not help. Take a photo with your camera app and load it with Image instead.

title: Troubleshooting
heading: The art looks stretched or squashed
text: - Leave Match the output font on in Fine tuning › Shape , so the cell shape matches the font. - If you pasted the art somewhere else, use a monospaced font there too; a proportional font breaks the columns. - If Lock row count is on, the row count no longer follows the picture. Turn it off.

title: Troubleshooting
heading: The art looks like a negative
text: The characters with the most ink should stand for the dark parts on light paper, and the light parts on dark paper. Check Invert for dark paper . Once you have changed it yourself, it no longer follows the paper colour automatically.

title: Troubleshooting
heading: The art is too dark, too light or flat
text: - Try Gamma : above 1 lightens the mid-tones, below 1 darkens them. - Raise Contrast . - Look at Character frequency in Analysis : a spike at one end means the tones are crushed. - Try the Line art or Bold look for strong shapes, or Fine for subtle tones.

title: Troubleshooting
heading: Smooth areas show bands
text: Turn on Floyd-Steinberg or Ordered (Bayer) dithering, or choose a longer set such as Detailed . The Compare tab shows which sets are not ordered light to dark.

title: Troubleshooting
heading: Colour does not show
text: - Under Colour , choose From image . Colour shows in the HTML , Canvas and SVG renders, not in Text . - With Rotate 90° , Border , Frame or Thin out on, the Canvas and SVG renders fall back to one colour. Turn those off for colour art.

title: Troubleshooting
heading: Filters do nothing
text: The HTML render shows the art before filters. Switch to Text , Canvas or SVG . Brighten , Darken and Noise work on Standard-set characters, so with other sets they change little or mix Standard characters in.

title: Troubleshooting
heading: The PNG, SVG or HTML download does not match the art
text: Those downloads can reuse an earlier render. Before downloading, select the matching render on the Lab tab: Canvas for PNG, SVG for SVG, HTML for HTML. Then download again.

title: Troubleshooting
heading: The ANSI download says to turn colour on
text: The ANSI file carries the picture's colours, so it needs From image . For plain characters, use the TXT download or Copy .

title: Troubleshooting
heading: Export all gave me five files, not six
text: That is how it works at present: Export all six downloads TXT, PNG, SVG, JSON and CSV. Download the HTML and ANSI files from their own cards. If only one file arrived, allow the page to download several files when your browser asks.

title: Troubleshooting
heading: Full screen shows no colour
text: Full screen shows the plain characters for every render except Canvas . Switch to Canvas first to see the colour art full screen. Close full screen with × .

title: Troubleshooting
heading: The Analysis charts are empty
text: Convert something first; the charts describe the last conversion. If they are still blank, switch to another tab and back.

title: Troubleshooting
heading: Conversion is slow or lags behind the sliders
text: Lower Detail , switch Sampling to Bilinear or Point / Nearest , turn off dithering, or use the Text render. The Render timeline chart and Run benchmark show the effect.

title: Frequently asked questions
heading: Are my pictures uploaded?
text: No. Pictures are read and converted in your browser and never leave your device. Downloads are built on your device too. See [Privacy](../others/privacy.md).

title: Frequently asked questions
heading: Do I need an account?
text: No. The generator works without signing in.

title: Frequently asked questions
heading: Is it really ASCII?
text: Only the Standard , Detailed and Minimal sets use plain ASCII characters. Blocks , Symbols , Lines and Braille use Unicode characters, which need a font that has them and may not display in every terminal or app.

title: Frequently asked questions
heading: Which settings give the best result?
text: Start with a look: Classic for photos, Line art for logos and drawings, Blocks for small, bold art, Fine for large, detailed art. Then adjust Detail for the space you have. Pictures with a clear subject and strong contrast convert best.

title: Frequently asked questions
heading: How wide should the art be?
text: It depends on where it goes. A README or chat message fits 60 to 100 columns; a terminal is often 80 to 120 columns wide; a poster or a PNG can go up to 300.

title: Frequently asked questions
heading: Can I keep the colours?
text: Yes, with From image . Colour survives in the HTML, PNG (from the Canvas render), SVG and ANSI downloads. Plain text and Copy carry no colour; Copy for terminal does.

title: Frequently asked questions
heading: Can I make animated ASCII art?
text: Not on this page. An animated GIF is converted as one still frame, and the webcam source cannot currently be used on the site.

title: Frequently asked questions
heading: Can I convert text into big letters?
text: Yes. Choose Text as the source, type a word, and pick a font, size and weight. The word is drawn and then converted. Batch on the Export tab measures a whole list of words.

title: Frequently asked questions
heading: Why does my text look wrong when I paste it?
text: The place you pasted into is probably using a proportional font. Put the art in a code block or set a monospaced font there.

title: Frequently asked questions
heading: Can I load a JSON file back in?
text: No. The JSON records the settings and the art, but the page has no import. You can save the art and settings to your Library instead; see [Copy, export and batch](export.md).

title: Frequently asked questions
heading: Does it work on a phone?
text: Yes. On narrow screens the art comes first and the controls follow. Pasting and dragging depend on the phone's browser; Choose a file always works.

title: Glossary
text: Term Meaning --- --- ANSI colour codes Escape sequences that terminals read as colour instructions. The ANSI download uses 24-bit (true colour) codes. Area average A sampling method that averages every pixel under a character cell. The page labels it SAT, after the summed-area table that makes it fast. Bayer matrix A fixed grid of thresholds used for ordered dithering, here 4 × 4 or 8 × 8. Bilinear sampling Reads a cell's value by blending the four nearest pixels. Braille pattern One of the 256 characters made of up to eight raised dots, used here as fine texture. Cell aspect A character cell's width divided by its height. Used to keep the art in proportion. Character set, ramp The characters the art is drawn with, ordered from least ink to most. Density How much of a character's cell is covered by ink, from 0 to 1. Dithering Spreading the rounding error between cells so that smooth tones appear as texture rather than bands. Edge-aware selection Swapping in a thin line character where the picture has a strong edge. Floyd–Steinberg An error-diffusion dithering method that passes each cell's error to its neighbours. Gamma A curve applied to brightness before conversion. Here, above 1 lightens the mid-tones. Glyph A single character as drawn by a font. Luminosity (Rec.601) A brightness formula that weights red, green and blue as the eye does, green most. Monospaced font A font in which every character has the same width, so columns line up. Monotonic Of a character set: each character has at least as much ink as the one before it. Point sampling Reads a cell's value from a single pixel. Fastest, but can shimmer on fine detail. Sobel operator A standard way to measure how quickly brightness changes, used to find edges. True colour 24-bit colour, about 16.7 million colours.

title: Limits and accuracy
heading: Size limits
text: Limit Value --- --- Image file 20 MB Image size used Up to 4,000 pixels a side and 12 megapixels; larger pictures are scaled down Width of the art 20 to 300 characters Locked row count 10 to 300 rows Custom ramp 2 to 200 characters Render timeline The last 100 conversions

title: Limits and accuracy
heading: Sources
text: - The webcam source cannot currently be used on auricartisan.com, because the site does not allow camera access on its pages. - An animated GIF is converted as a single still frame. - TIFF opens only in browsers that can display TIFF images. - The Text source draws with fonts installed on your device; a missing font is replaced by another.

title: Limits and accuracy
heading: Fonts decide how the art looks
text: Character art depends on a monospaced font. The same characters look different in different fonts, and wrong in a proportional one. Match the output font measures the chosen output font to keep proportions right, but the place you paste the art into uses its own font. The glyph density measurements in Analysis and Compare are made by drawing characters with the fonts on your device, so they can differ slightly from one computer to another.

title: Limits and accuracy
heading: Colour
text: - Text and Copy carry no colour. Colour needs the HTML, Canvas or SVG render, or the ANSI file. - The HTML render shows the art before filters and Thin out . - With colour on, filters that change the shape ( Rotate 90° , Border , Frame ) and Thin out make the Canvas, SVG and ANSI output fall back to one colour, and Flip X and Flip Y do not move the colours with the characters.

title: Limits and accuracy
heading: Filters
text: Brighten , Darken and Noise are built around the Standard characters. With other sets, Brighten and Darken change only the characters they know, and Noise adds Standard characters. Thin out removes repeated characters, so rows become uneven and the picture skews.

title: Limits and accuracy
heading: Edge-aware selection
text: Edge-aware selection can only use the line characters in the current set, and chooses by brightness, not by the direction of the edge. It has no effect with the Blocks, Minimal, Symbols, Lines or Braille sets.

title: Limits and accuracy
heading: Downloads
text: - The PNG, SVG and HTML downloads can reuse an earlier render unless the matching render is showing. See [Copy, export and batch](../docs/export.md). - Export all six downloads five files; the HTML and ANSI files are separate. - The SVG made from an HTML render embeds web content inside the SVG, which some design apps cannot open. The SVG made from the SVG render uses plain text elements. - The JSON file does not contain the source picture and cannot be loaded back into the page.

title: Limits and accuracy
heading: The benchmark
text: Run benchmark times ten conversions in your browser. Timings depend on your device, your browser and whatever else it is doing, so compare settings on the same device in the same session rather than across devices.

title: Basic Color Tools
text: Basic Color Tools is a workspace for everyday colour work on the Auric Artisan website. It brings seven small tools together on one page: Palette Studio , Palette Remix , Gradient Maker , Color Picker , Color Battle , Collage Maker and Quick Converter . Each tool opens as a floating panel with a controls sidebar on the left and a work area on the right. You can keep up to five panels open at once, move and resize them, dock them, and switch between them without leaving the page. The same folder also documents the Colour Tools workbench: fourteen further floating tools (such as Color Inspector , Contrast System and CMYK Soft-Proof ) that you can open on any page of the site from the right-click menu, with Ctrl + Shift + C , or by adding ?color= to a page address. When a page cannot open those tools, the site sends you to Basic Color Tools instead, so the two belong together. Everything runs in your browser. Palettes, gradients, colours and collages are computed on your device, images you add are read locally, and your preferences (favourites, level, last view) are remembered in your browser's local storage. You can save results to your Auric Artisan Library and reopen them in the right tool later.

title: Basic Color Tools
heading: Who it is for
text: - Designers who need a quick palette, gradient or colour conversion without opening a large application. - Front-end developers who want CSS, SCSS, Tailwind or JSON output for a palette or gradient. - Accessibility reviewers who want contrast ratios, WCAG pass levels and colour-vision previews next to the palette they are building. - Students and colour enthusiasts who want to see a colour in many formats and colour spaces at once.

title: Basic Color Tools
heading: Where to find it
text: - Page: https://auricartisan.com/tool/basic-tools/ (the short address https://auricartisan.com/basic-tools also opens it). - The Colour Tools workbench: right-click anywhere on a page of the site and use the Colour tools group, or press Ctrl + Shift + C . - No sign-in is needed to use the tools. Saving to the Library uses your Library; see [Import, export and the Library](docs/import-export-and-library.md).

title: Basic Color Tools
heading: Quick start
text: 1. Open https://auricartisan.com/tool/basic-tools/. The page opens on the Workspace view. 2. In the Open a tool list on the left, select Palette Studio . It opens as a panel on the stage to the right. 3. Select Generate (or press Space while the panel is focused) until you like the palette. 4. Hover over a colour and select the lock button to keep it, then generate again: locked colours stay put. 5. Open the Contrast Matrix or WCAG Pairs tab in the panel to check contrast between your colours. 6. In the Export section of the sidebar, select CSS to copy the palette as CSS custom properties, or PNG to download an image of it. 7. Open Gradient Maker from the list as well. Both panels stay open side by side; drag a title bar to arrange them. 8. Select Save to Library , the floating button near the bottom-right corner of the page, to keep the focused panel's result for later.

title: Basic Color Tools
heading: What you can do
text: - Generate palettes from thirteen harmony and accessibility modes, lock colours, edit them in OKLCH and extract colours from an image. - Remix a set of seed colours into four styled variant palettes. - Build linear, radial and conic gradients with any number of stops, perceptual interpolation and easing, then export CSS, SVG, PNG (1600 px or 4K), JSON or a Tailwind snippet. - Pick one colour and read it in HEX, RGB, HSL, HSV, OKLCH, Lab, XYZ and CMYK, with harmonies, colour-vision previews and contrast against common backgrounds. - Score two palettes against each other for contrast, perceptual separation and colour-vision resilience. - Compose local images into one of 29 collage layouts and export a 4K PNG. - Convert any colour between fourteen notations and compare two colours by ΔE and contrast. - Open fourteen more colour tools over any page through the Colour Tools workbench. - Save results to your Library and reopen them later in the matching tool.

title: Getting started with Basic Color Tools
text: This guide takes you from opening the page to exporting a checked palette. It takes about five minutes.

title: Getting started with Basic Color Tools
heading: Open the page
text: 1. Go to https://auricartisan.com/tool/basic-tools/ in a current desktop or mobile browser. JavaScript must be enabled. 2. Wait for the page to load. You see the title Basic Color Tools , a short description, and a row of labels: 4 Categories , 7 Tools , Palette Remix · Color Battle , Sidebar + Panel Layout and In-page Floating Panels . 3. Below the title is a row of three view buttons: Workspace , Catalogue and Panels . The page opens on Workspace the first time, and on the view you used last after that.

title: Getting started with Basic Color Tools
heading: A tour of the screen
text: View What it shows --- --- Workspace A launcher list on the left and a stage on the right. Tools you open appear as panels on the stage. This is where you work. Catalogue A searchable grid of tool cards with a category filter, a level switch, favourites and a copy-link button. Use it to browse and filter. Panels A list of the panels that are open, each with its state, and a reminder of what the panel title-bar buttons do. - Open a tool (left column) lists every tool the catalogue currently shows, grouped by category: Generate , Pick , Compose and Convert . Each row has a small colour band, the tool name, an Advanced label on advanced tools, and the word open when that tool already has a panel. - Panels (left column, below the list) shows how many panels are open out of five, as a number and a bar. It tells you how much room is left ("Room for 3 more.") or that you have reached the ceiling. Every open panel is listed with its state: Floating , Docked or Maximised . Select one to bring it back to the front. - The stage (right) is where panels open. Before you open anything it shows Nothing open yet. and a short explanation. Panels stay inside the stage while you work in this view. On screens narrower than about 1,100 pixels the launcher column sits above the stage instead of beside it. Every tool opens in the same kind of window: - A title bar with the tool's name and category, and four buttons: Open another instance (duplicate), Minimize , Maximize or restore , and Close . - A controls sidebar on the left with the tool's inputs and export buttons. - A main area on the right with the result, often split into tabs. - A resize handle in the bottom-right corner. On a narrow screen the sidebar and main area stack vertically inside the panel, and the panel body scrolls. A floating Save to Library button sits near the bottom-right corner of the page. It saves the result of the focused panel to your Library. See [Import, export and the Library](import-export-and-library.md).

title: Getting started with Basic Color Tools
heading: Your first palette
text: 1. In Open a tool , select Palette Studio . A panel opens on the stage with five colour strips in the main area. 2. Select Generate in the sidebar. Five new colours replace the old ones. You can also press Space while the panel is focused and your cursor is not in a text box or list. 3. Open the Harmony list and choose Analogous . The palette regenerates as neighbouring hues. 4. Hover over the second colour strip. Small buttons appear at its top. Select the lock button. The strip is marked as locked. 5. Select Generate a few more times. The locked colour stays; the others change. 6. Select + Add to add a sixth colour. A palette holds between two and nine colours. 7. Select the main area's Contrast Matrix tab. A table shows the WCAG contrast ratio of every pair of colours, colour-coded from fail to AAA. 8. Open the CVD Preview list in the sidebar and choose Deuteranopia . The strips now show how the palette may look to someone with deuteranopia. Your real colour values are unchanged; set the list back to Normal vision when you are done. 9. In the Export section, select CSS . The palette is copied to your clipboard as CSS custom properties, and a short CSS copied message appears. Result: a palette you generated, locked and checked, copied as code: css :root { --color-1: 3F6E8C; --color-2: 5B8A74; --color-3: A3B86A; --color-4: D9C27A; --color-5: E89F6B; --color-6: B5655C; } The colours above are only an example; yours will differ.

title: Getting started with Basic Color Tools
heading: Work with two tools at once
text: 1. With Palette Studio open, select Gradient Maker in Open a tool . A second panel opens, slightly offset from the first. 2. Drag the Gradient Maker title bar to move the panel. Drag the corner handle to make it smaller. 3. Select anywhere on the Palette Studio panel. It comes to the front. 4. Select Minimize on the Gradient Maker title bar. The panel is hidden from the stage, and the Panels list on the left shows it as Docked . Its work is kept. 5. Select Gradient Maker in the Panels list (or select Gradient Maker again in Open a tool ). It returns at its previous size and position, with your stops as you left them. Result: two tools on screen, and you know how to arrange, dock and restore them. For more, read [Workspace and panels](workspace-and-panels.md).

title: Import, export and the Library
text: Open panels in Basic Color Tools are not kept when you reload or leave the page. To keep your work, copy it, download it, or save it to your Auric Artisan Library. This guide lists every way in and out.

title: Import, export and the Library
heading: Bringing colours and images in
text: Into How Accepts --- --- --- Palette Studio From Image Any image file your browser can open. Colours are extracted on your device. Palette Studio Select a HEX label on a strip Any colour, through the site colour picker. Palette Remix Seed colors box HEX, rgb() , rgba() , hsl() , hsla() , hsv() , oklch() , separated by lines, spaces, commas, semicolons or vertical bars. Color Battle Team A and Team B boxes Same as Palette Remix, up to nine colours per team. Gradient Maker Stop HEX boxes and colour wells Three- or six-digit HEX, or the browser's picker. Color Picker HEX box, colour well, Pick eyedropper HEX; any pixel on screen where the eyedropper is supported. Quick Converter Input box, colour well HEX, rgb() , rgba() , hsl() , hsla() , hsv() , oklch() . Collage Maker + Add Images , or select a cell Image files from your device. Any tool Your Library Saved palettes, gradients and colours reopen in the matching tool. See below. Colours you type in any of the text boxes are converted to sRGB HEX codes. Values outside the sRGB range are clipped.

title: Import, export and the Library
heading: Copy and download formats
text: Button Kind Output --- --- --- Share Copy A link with the HEX codes after palette= CSS Copy CSS custom properties --color-1 … SCSS Copy Sass variables $color-1 … TW Copy Tailwind extend.colors snippet with palette-1 … JSON Copy Array of colour objects with metrics SVG Download palette.svg , 1200 × 240 PNG Download palette.png , 1200 × 240 ASE Copy Tab-separated text lines Examples: css :root { --color-1: D3AF37; --color-2: 1A1A2E; } scss $color-1: D3AF37; $color-2: 1A1A2E; text extend: { colors: { "palette-1": " D3AF37", "palette-2": " 1A1A2E" } } json [ { "hex": " D3AF37", "rgb": { "r": 211, "g": 175, "b": 55 }, "oklch": { "L": 0.766, "C": 0.138, "H": 91.6 }, "lab": { "L": 72.75, "a": 0.95, "b": 62.79 }, "luminance": 0.448, "bestText": { "hex": " 000000", "ratio": 9.96, "label": "dark", "passes": true }, "locked": false } ] For role palettes each object also has role , token , pairWith , target and note . The real output carries more decimal places than shown here. The ASE text looks like this, with tab characters between the parts: text Color 1 D3AF37 RGB(211, 175, 55) Color 2 1A1A2E RGB(26, 26, 46) It is plain text, not a binary Adobe Swatch Exchange file. Every row on the Formats tab (Color Picker) and the Convert tab (Quick Converter) has its own copy button. Quick Converter's CSS oklch() , CSS oklab() and CSS lab() rows are ready for stylesheets. Button Kind Output --- --- --- Copy winner Copy The winning team's HEX codes, one per line (Team A in a draw) Copy report Copy A short text report with the result and both scores Swatch Copy One HEX code Button Kind Output --- --- --- Export PNG (4K) Download collage.png , 3,840 pixels wide when the preview is at least 800 pixels wide Every copy button shows a short message such as Copied , CSS copied or JSON copied near the bottom of the page. If your browser blocks clipboard access, nothing is copied; see [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md).

title: Import, export and the Library
heading: The palette share link
text: Palette Studio's Share button copies a link like this: text https://auricartisan.com/tool/basic-tools/ palette=D3AF37-1A1A2E-F5DEB3-0F172A-FFFFFF The HEX codes are listed after palette= , without signs and separated by hyphens. Opening the link opens Basic Color Tools, but the page does not rebuild the palette from it automatically. Use the link as a compact record: copy the codes and paste them into Palette Remix, Color Battle or Quick Converter. The Catalogue's Copy link button copies the page address as it is in your browser.

title: Import, export and the Library
heading: Save to Library
text: The Save to Library button floats near the bottom-right corner of the page. On narrow screens it shows only its icon. 1. Focus the panel you want to save by selecting it. 2. Select Save to Library . 3. A save window opens listing what will be saved. For each item you can edit the Name and Description . You can also choose a Collection (or leave it Unfiled ) and add Tags (comma-separated) for all items. 4. Select Save to Library in the window, or press Ctrl + Enter ( Cmd + Enter on a Mac). Select Cancel to close without saving. Result: a message such as Saved "Palette · 5 colors (analogous)" appears, and the item is in your Library. What each tool saves: Focused panel Saved as --- --- Palette Studio One palette, with the harmony mode and CVD preview setting. Palette Remix Four palettes, one per remix set, named after the set. Gradient Maker One gradient, with its CSS, stops, type, angle, interpolation and easing. Color Picker One colour, with its formats and harmony colours. Color Battle Two palettes, Team A and Team B , each remembering both teams and the result. Quick Converter One colour, with every format. Collage Maker Nothing from the collage. Export the PNG instead. No panel open, or only Collage Maker A Basic Tools workspace bookmark that records your level setting. Save acts on the focused panel. Docked (minimised) panels are not saved. If there is nothing to save, a message says Nothing to save yet — try creating something first.

title: Import, export and the Library
heading: Reopening saved items
text: You can reopen items from your Library in Basic Color Tools. The item opens in a fresh panel of the tool that suits it, replacing any panel of that tool that is already open: Saved item Reopens in --- --- A palette saved from Palette Studio Palette Studio ( Loaded N colors from library ) A remix set Palette Remix, as seed colours ( Loaded remix from library ) A gradient Gradient Maker ( Loaded gradient from library ) A colour saved from Color Picker Color Picker ( Loaded color from library ) A colour saved from Quick Converter Quick Converter ( Loaded color from library ) A Color Battle team Color Battle, with both teams ( Loaded teams from library ) A palette, gradient or colour saved from another tool Palette Studio, Gradient Maker or Color Picker, by type A saved analysis run from the URL Analyzer Palette Studio, with the colours of the audited page Because a restore opens a fresh panel, any unsaved work in the replaced panel is lost. For how to browse, organise and send items from the Library, see the [Library Kit](../../../../kits/library-kit/README.md).

title: Workspace and panels
text: Basic Color Tools is a panel workspace. You open tools as floating windows called panels, keep several on screen, and arrange them as you like. This guide explains the three views of the page, the catalogue's filters, and every way to handle a panel. A panel is a movable, resizable window inside the page. It holds one tool. Panels are not browser windows or tabs, so they disappear when you reload or leave the page.

title: Workspace and panels
heading: The three views
text: The row of buttons under the page title switches between three views. The page remembers the view you used last, in your browser's local storage, and opens on it next time. The first visit opens on Workspace . View Use it to --- --- Workspace Open tools from a short list and work with them on a stage. Catalogue Browse tool cards, search, filter by category and level, and mark favourites. Panels See which panels are open and in what state, and read what each title-bar button does. Open panels are never closed by switching views. In the Workspace view they sit inside the stage. In the Catalogue and Panels views they float over the whole page. When you return to Workspace they move back into the stage.

title: Workspace and panels
heading: The Workspace view
text: The Open a tool list on the left shows the tools, grouped under their category names. The number next to the heading is how many tools the list shows. - Each row shows a small colour band that hints at what the tool makes, the tool's name, and an Advanced label for the three advanced tools. - A row reads open when that tool already has a panel. - Select a row to open the tool. If the tool is already open, its panel comes to the front instead, and a docked panel is restored. The list mirrors what the Catalogue currently shows. If you searched or filtered the Catalogue (for example by level or by Favorites ), the Workspace list shows the same subset. Clear the Catalogue filters to see all seven tools again. The Panels section under the list shows how many panels are open, out of a maximum of five, as a number and a bar. - While there is room it reads, for example, Room for 3 more. - At five it reads That is the ceiling. Close or dock one before opening another. - Each open panel is listed with its state: Floating , Docked or Maximised . Select an entry to bring that panel back to the front, restoring it if it is docked. The stage is the large surface on the right. Panels open inside it and cannot be dragged outside it. Maximize makes a panel fill the stage. When nothing is open the stage shows Nothing open yet. with a short explanation. On screens narrower than about 1,100 pixels the launcher column moves above the stage.

title: Workspace and panels
heading: The Catalogue view
text: The Catalogue is a grid of tool cards under a single filter bar. Control What it does --- --- Basic Tools A link that reloads the Basic Color Tools page. Search box Filters cards as you type. It matches tool names, summaries and tags; every word you type must appear. Placeholder: Search palette, remix, battle, gradient, picker, collage, converter... Clear Empties the search box and shows all cards again. Category list Shows one category: All Tools , Generate , Pick , Compose , Convert , Favorites or Open Panels . Level Three buttons: Basic , Advanced and Both . See below. Count Shows how many cards are visible out of the total, for example 4 of 7 . Copy link Copies the page address to your clipboard. The label briefly changes to Copied . Quick start button The round information button. Shows or hides the quick start note. The quick start note says: pick any tool card to open it as a movable floating panel; each panel has a controls sidebar on the left and an interactive workspace on the right; open up to five at once, drag to reposition, resize from the corner, maximize to full screen, or close with the × button. The × on the note hides it and the page remembers that choice. The level switch filters tools by depth. Both is the default. Level Tools shown --- --- Basic Palette Studio, Gradient Maker, Color Picker, Quick Converter Advanced Palette Remix, Color Battle, Collage Maker Both All seven The page remembers your level in your browser's local storage. Category Tools --- --- Generate Palette Studio, Palette Remix, Gradient Maker Pick Color Picker, Color Battle Compose Collage Maker Convert Quick Converter With All Tools or Favorites selected, cards are grouped under category headings, each with a count such as 3 tools . The page remembers the category you chose. Each card shows the category, the tool name, a colour band, a one-line summary and tags: the category, Basic or Advanced , up to three topic tags, and ● Open when the tool has a panel. - Select a card to open the tool, or to bring its existing panel forward. - Hold Shift , Ctrl or Cmd while you select a card to open another instance even if one is already open. - Select the star on a card to add it to Favorites or remove it. Favourites are saved in your browser's local storage. If no card matches your search, the grid shows No basic tools match. If Favorites is empty it shows No favorites yet. with a reminder to select the star on a card. Choose Open Panels in the category list to see a card for each open panel. A card reads Floating workspace is active or Minimized in dock , and shows Maximized when the panel is maximised. Select a card to restore and focus that panel. With nothing open it shows No panels open.

title: Workspace and panels
heading: The Panels view
text: The Panels view has two cards. - Open panels lists every panel with its name, category and state ( floating , docked or maximised ) and a count such as 2 of 5 . With nothing open it says No panels open. The Workspace tab is where you start one. - What the bar does explains the four title-bar buttons: Duplicate makes a second copy with its own state; Minimise parks the panel in the dock and keeps its work; Maximise gives it the whole page and back; Close frees one of the five slots. This view is for reading. To bring a panel back, use the Workspace Panels list or the Catalogue's Open Panels category.

title: Workspace and panels
heading: Working with panels
text: - Title bar : a grip, the tool's name and category, and four buttons. - Controls sidebar on the left and main area on the right. When the panel is narrow they stack, and the panel body scrolls. - Resize handle in the bottom-right corner. - Tabs across the top of the main area in most tools. Select a tab to switch what the main area shows. Button Tooltip What it does --- --- --- Duplicate Open another instance Opens a second panel of the same tool with its own, separate state. − Minimize Hides the panel and docks it. Its work is kept. The Workspace Panels list shows it as docked. □ Maximize or restore Fills the stage (Workspace view) or the browser window (other views). Select again to return to the previous size. × Close Closes the panel and discards its work. 1. Drag the title bar to move a panel. Panels cannot be dragged while maximised. 2. Drag the bottom-right handle to resize. The smallest size is 480 by 380 pixels, or the available space if that is smaller. 3. Double-click the title bar to maximise or restore. 4. Select anywhere on a panel to bring it to the front. The front panel is the focused panel: keyboard shortcuts and Save to Library act on it. Panels always stay inside the stage or the window with a small margin. If you make the browser window smaller, open panels are pulled back inside it. When the keyboard focus is inside a panel, Escape restores a maximised panel to its previous size. If the panel is not maximised, Escape closes it and its work is lost. Select outside the panel first if you only want to leave a text box. Selecting a tool that is already open brings the existing panel forward. To get a second copy, select the title bar's Open another instance button, or hold Shift , Ctrl or Cmd while you select the tool's card in the Catalogue. Each copy keeps its own colours and settings. Up to five panels can be open at once. If you open a sixth, the panel that was opened earliest is closed automatically to make room, and its work is lost. Save anything you want to keep to your Library first, or close a panel yourself. - Kept in your browser's local storage: your last view, level, category, favourites, and whether you dismissed the quick start note. - Not kept: open panels and their contents. Reloading or leaving the page closes them. To keep a result, copy or download it, or use Save to Library . See [Import, export and the Library](import-export-and-library.md).
